title: Project governance & governance boards
blurb: What project governance is, who sits on the governance board, and which decisions the board takes rather than the project manager.
question: At the end of definition, a council's steering group reviews whether its waste-collection app is still worth building after a government grant was cut. Who sits on that group, and why is this their decision rather than the project manager's?

teach.body: APM describes project governance as the framework of authority and accountability that defines and controls the outputs, outcomes and benefits from projects. In plain English: governance sets out how decisions are made and who makes them. It answers questions like 'who can approve this?', 'who can stop the project?' and 'who must be told?', so the project stays justified, aligned to strategy and under control from start to finish.

teach.caption: Direction and decisions flow down; progress reports and escalations flow up. The board directs, the project manager manages, the team delivers.

teach.h: Who sits on the governance board

root.label: Governance board
root.sub: also called project board or steering group

children.label: Senior user reps
children.sub: speak for those who will use it

children.label: Senior supplier reps
children.sub: speak for those who build it

teach.caption: The project manager attends to report and advise but is not a decision-making member of the board.

items: Gives direction to the project and the project manager.
Makes the key decisions, including on issues the sponsor brings to it.
Approves the project at decision gates before the next phase starts.
Ensures the project stays viable: the business case still justifies it.
Ensures the project stays aligned to the organisation's strategy.

teach.h: Decision gates along a linear life cycle
teach.caption: Gates are governance control points between phases, where the sponsor or board decides whether the project continues.

root.label: Decision gate review
root.sub: Is the business case still viable? Are we ready?

teach.caption: Stopping an unviable project early is a success of governance, not a failure: it saves money for better uses.

teach.body: The council's Head of Environmental Services is sponsor and chairs the steering group. A crew supervisor sits as senior user; the app developer's account director sits as senior supplier. At the definition gate, the project manager reports that a government grant has been cut. The board reviews the business case, decides on 're-plan' and asks for a smaller first release. The project manager then updates the plan to match.

teach.text: Don't confuse the governance board with the PMO. The board DECIDES and directs (approves gates, keeps the project viable). The PMO SUPPORTS governance with reporting and assurance but makes none of those decisions. And the board does not run the project day to day: that's the project manager.

items: Governance: the framework of authority and accountability that defines and controls outputs, outcomes and benefits.
Governance board, project board or steering group: chaired by the sponsor, with senior user and supplier representatives.
The board gives direction, makes key decisions and approves at decision gates (go, no-go, hold, re-plan).
It keeps the project viable and aligned to strategy; the project manager manages within the limits it sets.

summary: You can now define project governance, describe the make-up and role of the governance board, and explain how decision gates let the board continue, pause, re-plan or stop a project. You can also tell governance decisions apart from day-to-day management decisions.

A.q: Complete the statement: project governance is the framework of…
options: templates and tools for project managers
tasks and activities for each project team
requirements and features for the users
A.why: Governance is the framework of authority and accountability that defines and controls a project's outputs, outcomes and benefits.

whyNot.0: Templates and tools are provided by a PMO; they support governance but are not governance itself.
whyNot.1: Tasks and activities are captured in the work breakdown structure and schedule.
whyNot.3: Requirements and features are captured in a specification or, on iterative work, the product backlog.

A.q: Which is another common name for a project's governance board?
A.why: The governance board is also called the project board or steering group.

whyNot.1: A project office (PMO) supports projects; it is not the decision-making board.
whyNot.2: The delivery team carries out the work under the project manager.
whyNot.3: A work package is a unit of work in the WBS, not a group of people.

A.q: Who normally sits on the governance board alongside the sponsor?
options: Every team member and the PMO
A.why: The board is chaired by the sponsor and includes senior user and senior supplier representatives, so both sides of the project have a voice in decisions.

whyNot.0: Team members deliver the work and the PMO supports; neither sits on the board as a decision-maker.
whyNot.1: Users are represented by a senior user, not by people chosen at random.
whyNot.2: The supplier's delivery staff do the work; a senior supplier representative sits on the board.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are functions of the governance board?
1) Approving progress at decision gates
2) Updating the project schedule
3) Ensuring the project stays aligned to strategy
4) Producing the work packages
B.why: Approving at decision gates (1) and keeping the project aligned to strategy (3) are governance board functions.

whyNot.0: Both 2 and 4 are project manager and team tasks.
whyNot.2: Producing work packages (4) is planning work for the project manager and team.
whyNot.3: Updating the schedule (2) is the project manager's job.

B.q: Which list gives the possible outcomes of a decision gate review?
B.why: At a gate the sponsor or board decides to go on, stop (no-go), hold, or send the project back to re-plan.

whyNot.0: These are responses to threats in risk management.
whyNot.1: These are the MoSCoW priorities used on iterative projects.
whyNot.2: This is a continuous improvement cycle, not a set of gate decisions.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a role of the governance board?
B.why: Allocating tasks is day-to-day management, which belongs to the project manager.

whyNot.0: Giving direction is a core board function.
whyNot.1: Approval at decision gates is a key governance control.
whyNot.3: The board makes sure the business case still justifies the project.

C.q: At the end of definition, the board learns a competitor has launched a near-identical product and the business case no longer stacks up. What is the most appropriate gate decision?
options: Go, as the plan is already approved
No-go: stop or redirect the project
Hold the gate until deployment ends
Let the team vote on whether to go on
C.why: If the business case is no longer viable, the board should stop or redirect the project rather than spend more on it.

whyNot.0: An approved plan does not justify continuing when the reason for the project has gone.
whyNot.2: Deployment cannot start while the gate is held, and holding does not address the lost justification.
whyNot.3: Gate decisions are a governance responsibility, not a team vote.

C.q: Why does the sponsor usually chair the governance board?
options: They are accountable for the project
They are the most expert specialist
They provide the PMO's standard templates
C.why: The sponsor is accountable for the project meeting its need and delivering benefits, so it makes sense for the sponsor to lead the board that directs it.

whyNot.1: The daily schedule is managed by the project manager.
whyNot.2: Specialist expertise comes from team members, not from the chair of the board.
whyNot.3: Templates come from the PMO, not the sponsor.

C.q: The sponsor, a senior user and a senior supplier jointly approve a change that moves the project's end date. This is an example of:
C.why: A board with authority making a decision beyond the project manager's tolerance is governance in action.

whyNot.0: Quality control inspects and tests outputs against acceptance criteria.
whyNot.1: Resource scheduling plans when resources are used; it does not authorise changes to the baseline.
whyNot.2: Team development is about how the team forms and performs.

reteach.title: Governance is the festival's organising committee
reteach.question: A town runs a summer music festival. A committee meets each month; an events manager runs everything in between. How does that mirror project governance?

blocks.body: The committee is chaired by the councillor who championed the festival and includes a residents' representative (the users) and the lead production company (the supplier). They decide whether the festival goes ahead, approve the budget and step in on big problems. The events manager books acts, manages crews and reports to them. Between meetings, the manager decides within agreed limits.

blocks.text: The committee never sets up the stage, and the events manager never decides on their own to cancel the festival. Governance decides; management delivers.

explain.body: Governance is the framework of authority and accountability that defines and controls a project's outputs, outcomes and benefits: how decisions are made and who makes them.

test.q: Project governance is mainly concerned with…
options: how decisions are made and by whom
how activities are sequenced in time
how the team is motivated and led
how costs are split into accounts
test.why: Governance defines how decisions are made and who makes them, giving authority and accountability a clear structure.

whyNot.3: Splitting costs into accounts is the cost breakdown structure.

explain.body: The board (project board or steering group) is chaired by the sponsor, with senior user and senior supplier representatives. It gives direction and makes the key decisions.

test.q: Who usually chairs the governance board?
test.why: The sponsor usually chairs the governance board.

whyNot.0: The project manager reports to the board but does not chair it.
whyNot.1: The PMO supports the board with information and assurance.
whyNot.3: A senior user represents users on the board but does not normally chair it.

explain.body: Between phases, the sponsor or board reviews the business case, progress and readiness, then decides: go, no-go, hold or re-plan. Gates stop unviable projects early.

test.q: The governance board meets at the end of a phase to hold a decision gate. What is that meeting mainly for?
options: Record the lessons learned after closure
Assign owners to each new risk
test.why: A decision gate is where the continuation of the project is decided, based on the business case, progress and readiness.

whyNot.0: Lessons learned are captured in the post-project review.
whyNot.2: Timesheets are a routine management matter, not a governance control point.
whyNot.3: Assigning risk owners happens in the risk response stage.

explain.body: The board decides whether the project is still worth doing and approves big changes. The project manager decides how to keep it on track, within the tolerances the governance arrangements allow.

test.q: Which decision belongs to the project manager rather than to governance?
options: Approving the project past the next gate
test.why: Re-sequencing tasks without breaching a tolerance is day-to-day management, which the project manager is authorised to do.

whyNot.0: Gate approval is a governance decision.
whyNot.1: Confirming strategic alignment is a board responsibility.
whyNot.2: Stopping a project is a governance decision taken by the sponsor or board.
